facts.statehood_note: Corydon was the first state capital; the capital moved to Indianapolis in 1825.
facts.name_origin: "Indiana" means "Land of the Indians." A trading company used the name in 1768 for a land claim, and Congress used it in 1800 when it created Indiana Territory.

government.chambers: Indiana Senate (50 senators, 4-year terms) and Indiana House of Representatives (100 representatives, 2-year terms). It is a part-time "citizen legislature" that has met every year since 1972.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; a governor may serve only 8 years in any 12-year period). The governor manages many state agencies and can veto bills passed by the General Assembly.
government.courts: Indiana Supreme Court (5 justices). When a seat opens, the governor chooses from three candidates picked by the Judicial Nominating Commission. Justices must win a retention election after two years, then serve 10-year terms. Indiana also has a Court of Appeals, a Tax Court, and circuit courts.
government.constitution: Indiana's first constitution was written at Corydon in June 1816 and banned slavery. The current constitution was adopted in 1851. As first written, its Article 13 barred Black people from coming into or settling in the state, and it denied Black men the vote; many of these rules were reversed after the Civil War.
government.kid_line: "WE DECLARE, That all people are created equal; that they are endowed by their CREATOR with certain inalienable rights;" (Indiana Constitution, Article 1, Section 1)

long_ago.about: From about 1000 to 1450, Mississippian people lived in a permanent town on the Ohio River near today's Evansville, where they farmed and stored corn and built twelve earthen mounds for ceremonies.
The Myaamia were one of the two largest nations in Indiana. After treaties in 1809, 1818, and 1826 took most of their land, they held reservations along the Wabash, Mississinewa, and Eel rivers.
The Potawatomi, the other large nation in Indiana, lived in northern Indiana. In three 1832 treaties they gave up more than 4 million acres in Indiana, and in 1838 most were forced west.
The Lenape (Delaware) settled in the White River and Whitewater River valleys; like most nations in Indiana, they were later removed west.
These nations also lived in what is now Indiana; most were removed west in the 1820s and 1830s.

today.about: A federally recognized nation (status affirmed by Congress in 1994) based in Dowagiac, Michigan, with reservation lands in ten counties across Michigan and Indiana; it opened Four Winds South Bend in Indiana in 2018.

first_peoples.today_note: The Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians stayed in the region during removal and is federally recognized today. The Miami Nation of Indians of the State of Indiana, based in Peru, Indiana, lost federal recognition in 1897 and has not regained it. The federally recognized Miami Tribe of Oklahoma has about 500 members living in Indiana. In 2000, more than 39,000 Native Americans from over 150 tribes lived in Indiana.
sites: Angel Mounds State Historic Site on the Ohio River near Evansville (about 600 acres, twelve mounds)
Chief Menominee statue near Twin Lakes and Plymouth (1909), the first monument to a Native American put up under a state or federal law, remembering the Potawatomi Trail of Death

history.event: After the Ice Age, Paleo-Indians arrive and hunt large animals such as mastodons.
Mississippian people farm corn and build twelve mounds at the town now called Angel Mounds on the Ohio River.
French fur traders set up trading posts, the first around 1702; in 1732 Sieur de Vincennes builds a post at Vincennes.
On February 25, George Rogers Clark captures Vincennes and Fort Sackville.
The Treaty of Greenville takes the first Native land in what becomes Indiana. On May 7, 1800, Congress creates Indiana Territory.
In the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne, Governor William Henry Harrison takes about 2.5 million acres from the Myaamia (Miami). On November 7, 1811, U.S. forces win the Battle of Tippecanoe.

Delegates at Corydon write a constitution that says, "There shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in this state." On December 11, Indiana becomes the 19th state, with Corydon as its capital.
The Treaty of St. Mary's takes central Indiana, about half the state, from the Myaamia (Miami).
The state capital moves from Corydon to Indianapolis.

In Newport (now Fountain City), Quakers Levi and Catharine Coffin shelter more than 1,000 freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad. Indiana is a free state, but freedom seekers are still not safe there.
On the Potawatomi Trail of Death, 859 Potawatomi, including Chief Menominee's Yellow River band, are forced about 660 miles from Twin Lakes to Kansas; 42 die, 28 of them children.
Many Myaamia (Miami) are forced to move by canal and steamboat from Peru, Indiana, to Kansas; less than half of the nation leaves, and many families stay on their own land.
A new state constitution includes Article 13, which says Black people may not come into or settle in Indiana, and it denies Black men the vote.
Indiana sends more than 208,000 soldiers to the Union Army. Lucy Higgs Nichols escapes slavery in 1862 and nurses Union soldiers. The Battle of Corydon is fought during Morgan's Raid.
After the Civil War, many of Indiana's laws against Black residents are reversed, though unfair treatment continues; by 1869, Radical Republicans lead the General Assembly.

trailblazers.name: Chief Menominee
trailblazers.text: Menominee was a Potawatomi chief and religious leader whose Yellow River band lived at Twin Lakes near Plymouth. He refused to accept the 1836 treaty that sold his band's land, saying, "I have not sold my lands. I will not sell them." In 1838 militia forced his people west on the Trail of Death; Indiana put up a statue of him in 1909.

trailblazers.name: Catharine and Levi Coffin
trailblazers.text: The Coffins left North Carolina because they opposed slavery and lived in Newport (now Fountain City) from 1826 to 1847. Catharine gathered food and organized a sewing society to make clothes, and their home sheltered more than 1,000 freedom seekers. Their house became a National Historic Landmark in 1966.

trailblazers.name: Lucy Higgs Nichols
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, Civil War nurse
trailblazers.text: Lucy Higgs Nichols was born enslaved in 1838. In 1862 she escaped to the camp of the 23rd Regiment, Indiana Volunteers, and worked as a nurse for its soldiers through many major battles of the Civil War. After the war she came to New Albany, Indiana, with the regiment's returning veterans.

trailblazers.name: Madam C.J. Walker
trailblazers.text: Born Sarah Breedlove in Louisiana, she built a hair-care company for African American women and became one of the first self-made women millionaires in America. She moved her business to Indianapolis in 1910 and gave money to Black colleges and community groups. Her company headquarters is now the Madame Walker Legacy Center.

trailblazers.name: May Wright Sewall
trailblazers.text: May Wright Sewall of Indiana chaired the executive committee of the National Woman Suffrage Association from 1882 to 1890. She helped found the National Council of Women in 1888 and served as its president from 1897 to 1899.

trailblazers.name: Dorothy Buell
trailblazers.text: Dorothy Buell, an English teacher from Ogden Dunes, joined the effort to protect the Indiana Dunes in 1949. Her work led to the Save the Dunes Council in 1952, and in 1958 she asked Senator Paul Douglas for help; Congress created Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore in 1966, now Indiana Dunes National Park.

trailblazers.name: Hurley C. Goodall
trailblazers.text: Born in Muncie, Hurley Goodall was one of the city's first two African American firefighters and the first Black person to win a seat on Muncie's school board. In 1978 he was elected to the Indiana House of Representatives.

landforms: Flat till plains in central Indiana, left by glaciers
Moraines and kettle lakes in the north
Rugged southern hills with exposed bedrock, caves, and limestone quarries
Lake Michigan sand dunes nearly 200 feet high
Hoosier Hill in Wayne County, the highest point (1,257 feet)
waters: Wabash River (state river; part of the Illinois border)
Lowest point (about 320 feet) where the Wabash meets the Ohio in Posey County
geography.regions: Glaciers flattened most of northern and central Indiana into farmland with lakes in the north, while southern Indiana has hills, caves, and limestone.

ecosystems.name: Lake Michigan dunes and wetlands
ecosystems.about: Indiana Dunes National Park has about 1,100 native plant species, including the threatened Pitcher's thistle, and holds 30% of Indiana's rare or endangered plant species.

ecosystems.name: Tallgrass prairie remnants
ecosystems.about: The dunes lie at the eastern edge of the tallgrass prairie peninsula and still hold high-quality patches of prairie.

ecosystems.name: Forests
ecosystems.about: Indiana Dunes holds plants of eastern deciduous (leaf-dropping) forests along with leftover patches of northern boreal forest plants. The tulip tree is the state tree.

science.weather: Indiana's climate is mostly humid continental, with a record high of 116°F (1936) and a record low of -36°F (1994). It is not in Tornado Alley, but it ranked eighth among tornado-prone states from 1950 to 2011.
science.resources: Indiana is known for limestone (used in the first statehouse at Corydon), steel, cars, and medicines, and its glacier-flattened plains are good farmland.
science.highlight: Indiana Dunes is called "the birthplace of American ecology." In 1899 botanist Henry Cowles published a study of Lake Michigan dune plants and how plant communities change over time (plant succession), earning the title "father of plant ecology," and the dunes became the 61st national park in 2019.

g3_ss.title: Indiana's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Indianapolis, Corydon, and the student's county among 92 counties; learn the 50-member Senate, 100-member House, governor, and 5-justice Supreme Court; read Article 1, Section 1.

g3_ss.title: Indiana's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Angel Mounds, then the Myaamia (Miami), Potawatomi, and Lenape homelands; meet the Pokagon Band and the Miami people in Indiana today.

g3_ss.title: Indiana Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Chief Menominee, Catharine Coffin, Lucy Higgs Nichols, Madam C.J. Walker, and Dorothy Buell; students make a trading card for each.

g45_ss.title: Indiana's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Paleo-Indians, Angel Mounds, the Myaamia and Potawatomi, treaties from Greenville to St. Mary's, the Trail of Death, and the 1846 Miami removal.

g45_ss.title: French Posts to Territory
g45_ss.plan: French traders at Vincennes, George Rogers Clark in 1779, Indiana Territory in 1800, Harrison's land treaties, and the Battle of Tippecanoe.

g45_ss.title: Free State, Unequal Laws, 1816 to 1877
g45_ss.plan: The 1816 slavery ban, the Coffins and the Underground Railroad, Article 13 of 1851, Indiana in the Civil War, and changes after the war.

g3_sci.title: Life on the Dunes
g3_sci.plan: How sand dunes form along Lake Michigan and which plants hold them in place; build a dune in a box with a fan.

g3_sci.title: Glaciers and Farmland
g3_sci.plan: How glaciers flattened central Indiana; compare flat till plains with the southern hills.

g3_sci.title: Limestone Builds Indiana
g3_sci.plan: What limestone is made of, where it is quarried, and buildings made from it, like the first statehouse at Corydon.

g45_sci.title: Plant Succession at the Dunes
g45_sci.plan: Follow Henry Cowles's dune studies and chart how plant communities change over time, from bare sand to forest.

g45_sci.title: Rocks, Caves, and Quarries
g45_sci.plan: Southern Indiana's bedrock, caves, and Salem limestone; how water shapes rock underground.

g45_sci.title: Indiana Weather Watch
g45_sci.plan: Record temperatures and Indiana's tornado risk; graph local weather and make a storm safety plan.
